messages.subject: A couple of feature requests
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yihui:

I wonder if it's possible to eventually get the following in knitr:

(i) the ability to comment out text/code so that knitr passes LaTeX %
leaders to the .tex file;
(ii) the ability to put captions in graphics without having to produce
a LaTeX figure environment.

The problem with LaTeX's floating figures in a document with a lot of
graphs is that once they start floating, they can get completely out
of whack relative to the text. I really like the way knitr positions
graphics, but it would be even better if one could place captions
below the graphs.

Think of these as wishlist items; since they're more on the LaTeX side
than the R side, I wouldn't be surprised if a 'good' solution would be
difficult to come by.

I really like the new docs on the web site - keep up the great work!

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] A couple of feature requests
messages.body_plain:
1. You are free to comment out code chunks, e.g.

% <<>>=
% # R code
% @

This will not be parsed by knitr. Currently it is not possible to
comment out inline R code with %, e.g.

% here is a piece of inline R code \Sexpr{pi}

will still be parsed and executed. This feature was requested in
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/110 but it looks difficult to
implement.

2. This is almost a LaTeX problem, and I cannot do much about it on
knitr's side. You can force a figure to ignore floating by
\begin{figure}[!h] or \usepackage{float} and \begin{figure}[H]. It is
pretty ticky to deal with LaTeX figure environments, and I think it is
the biggest lie of LaTeX (it frees us of worrying about styles so we
can focus on writing...).

A set of commands that I often use is:

\renewcommand{\textfraction}{0.05}
\renewcommand{\topfraction}{0.8}
\renewcommand{\bottomfraction}{0.8}
\renewcommand{\floatpagefraction}{0.75}

This can alleviate the problem a little bit. It tells LaTeX to give
more freedom to figures; it is often annoying that figures float to
the next page just because we make them slightly larger.

Besides that, make the plots as small as possible (especially the height).

Anyway, it is also possible to ask knitr to write something below the
figures (not using the figure environment) through chunk hooks, but
the main problem is you lose the figure numbers.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] A couple of feature requests
messages.body_plain:
I didn't expect this would be easy, but I thought I'd ask :) I've used
those LaTeX figure tricks, but when you have a lot of graphs with
little text between them, it doesn't take long before the figures and
the text become disconnected. I much prefer knitr's way of handling
them. I also use the \renewcommand{}'s you listed in my preamble on a
regular basis.

Thanks for the useful reply,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Yes, any options can be set globally via \SweaveOpts{}. Or if you want
it to be even more "global", you can change the default setting of
knitr permanently by opts_chunk$set(comment = NA) before you start to
knit() any documents.

BTW, I have been thinking of putting together a set of hook functions
for listings in knitr so that you only need to call something like
render_listings() to get listings output. I do not use listings very
often by myself, but I believe there must be a number of people
interested in this. I know you have been working on it, so I will be
happy to wrap up your listings hooks (including the LaTeX preamble
settings) into knitr in the next version if you like. Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui

})
@

messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Re: What is preferred way to specify graphics size?
messages.body_plain:
The built-in graphical devices only support three key arguments: width
(fig.width), height (fig.height) and dpi (dpi). I thought these three
were enough... If you want other arguments, you have to write a new
device function, e.g.

my_pdf = function(file, width, height) {
  pdf(file, width = width, height = height, pointsize =
opts_current$get('pointsize'))
}

The object opts_current gives you the chunk options for the current
chunk, so you can use any custom options in your hooks or device
functions, e.g.

<<pdf-with-pointsize, dev=my_pdf, width=5, height=4, pointsize=10>>=
plot(1)
@

For the caption problem, I have been thinking on how to deal with
commas as well. You can use other characters to replace commas when
writing the captions, and replace them back to commas in the hook to
get the real captions. For example, use ;; as , and I guess a neater
solution is to be able to escape the comma like \,. I will see what I
can do.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.body_plain:
You can override the default device by setting a global option like
\SweaveOpts{dev=your_dev_name}.

In fact you may not need to evaluate 'name' in @name; there is an
alternative way to do that. You can set

opts_knit$set(eval.opts = c('eval', 'echo', 'caption')) # see
http://yihui.name/knitr/options#package_options

then use

<<>>=
.fig.caption = 'a long long caption here'
<<my-caption, caption=.fig.caption>>=
@

In this case, the caption will be evaluated to the real character string.

messages.body_plain:
Sorry this is a bug in the object opts_current. It should have been
created _after_ the options have been evaluated. I have fixed it in
the development version: https://github.com/yihui/knitr Now you should
be able to use opts_current$get('caption') to get the real caption
string.

Or alternatively, you can use the argument 'options' in the hook
function; it is always the evaluated version.

knit_hooks$set(caption = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (!before) paste('\\caption{', options$caption, '}')
})

Theoretically 'options' in the hook function should be identical to
opts_current$get(), but due to that bug, they are not. The fix will
appear in v0.3 on CRAN about two weeks later.

Regards,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

I see the great value in this idea, and I have even thought hard about
it in the beginning of the knitr design. In fact this is what an ideal
knitting/weaving engine looks like in my mind, but later I still
surrendered to Sweave and adopted the current model (replace source
code with output).

Hadley's decumar package follows your idea, and the implementation is
roughly like this:

% begin_r_chunk
% opt1: value1
% opt2: value2
% # R code here
% rnorm(10)
% 1 + 1
% end_r_chunk

You write everything in comments, and after you have evaluated the
code, the output is put after the R code, and the source code is still
there in comments. Next time when you run the code again, only the
output is replaced. This model guarantees you always operate on one
single document.

This is why I complained about the WEB/Noweb/Sweave syntax in the end
of this page: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/ The traditional
model (<<>>= and @) not only broke the syntax of other document
formats, but also ignored this possibility of putting source code (in
comments) and output together.

Well, since you brought this back to me with a potential application,
I will reconsider this model again. It may not be terribly difficult
to implement, and one difficulty as I can see for the time being is
how to deal with inline R code. Thanks!

BTW, before I proceed, I think you may play with version control tools
for collaboration (like GIT or SVN), but everybody should only edit
the source document. If anyone wants to see the real output, he/she
has to compile it based on the current version of the source document.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Feature Request; Ability to knit an output file agaain ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The last paragraph of Yihui's note is important. One of the very
useful applications of Git is collaborative writing. One of the
participants controls the master document, and others can add
modifications by creating branches of the master and then placing
their changes in a branch. When one is finished, the branch is pushed
to GitHub and the participant sends a pull request to the owner of the
master branch. That person can then pull the (sets of) changes into
the master document, make additional modifications as necessary and
then push the result back to GitHub. The process is iterated to
convergence. Each new set of changes is placed in a separate branch.
By keeping changes in separate branches, it is possible to maintain a
revision history of who made which changes at which times. This
requires some education about how Git works, but it's something worth
considering.

HTH,
Dennis

On Thu, Feb 9, 2012 at 8:34 PM, Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Paul,
>
> I see the great value in this idea, and I have even thought hard about
> it in the beginning of the knitr design. In fact this is what an ideal
> knitting/weaving engine looks like in my mind, but later I still
> surrendered to Sweave and adopted the current model (replace source
> code with output).
>
> Hadley's decumar package follows your idea, and the implementation is
> roughly like this:
>
> % begin_r_chunk
> % opt1: value1
> % opt2: value2
> % # R code here
> % rnorm(10)
> % 1 + 1
> % end_r_chunk
>
> You write everything in comments, and after you have evaluated the
> code, the output is put after the R code, and the source code is still
> there in comments. Next time when you run the code again, only the
> output is replaced. This model guarantees you always operate on one
> single document.
>
> This is why I complained about the WEB/Noweb/Sweave syntax in the end
> of this page: http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/ The traditional
> model (<<>>= and @) not only broke the syntax of other document
> formats, but also ignored this possibility of putting source code (in
> comments) and output together.
>
> Well, since you brought this back to me with a potential application,
> I will reconsider this model again. It may not be terribly difficult
> to implement, and one difficulty as I can see for the time being is
> how to deal with inline R code. Thanks!
>
> BTW, before I proceed, I think you may play with version control tools
> for collaboration (like GIT or SVN), but everybody should only edit
> the source document. If anyone wants to see the real output, he/she
> has to compile it based on the current version of the source document.
>
> Regards,
> Yihui

>> Hello,
>>
>> I've got a particular scenario (use-case) in my head that knitr might
>> be great for.  I want to produce a report of an experiment that
>> several people are collaborating on.  I am doing the data analysis but
>> others are doing some of the intepretations and conclusions.  I want
>> to have a source file with R code in that I can run through a process
>> (sweave | knitr) to produce an output file with the results / tables /
>> graphs.  I will then share that with the others who may make changes
>> to the words, move things around or possibly change the R code
>> slightly.  I then want to periodically take that file and run my
>> process (sweave | knitr) on it again, which should update the
>> results / tabls / graphs from R but leave everything else as it was.
>>

>>

>>

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] par() being ignored in customized device
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] par() being ignored in customized device
messages.body_plain:
At the first glance, I thought this was a bug, but now I see the
misunderstanding. A device is only used to save plots _after_ the code
is executed; this is a slight difference with Sweave, as Sweave opens
a device, then runs the code and closes the device. In knitr, the
plots are first _recorded_, then saved, so par(bty) did not really go
into the recorded plot.

I recommend you to separate different functions apart: let a device
function only open a device, and let chunk hooks do the job of
executing R code before/after the chunk, e.g.

<<par-hook>>=
knit_hooks$set(par = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (!before) return()
  pars <- opts_current$get(c('bty', 'las'))
  do.call(par, pars)
})
@

<<plot-par, par=TRUE, bty=l, las=2>>=
plot(rnorm(100))
@

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Minimal Beamer example
messages.body_plain:
Hi knitr list,

I browsed the demo list of knitr to get an example that uses beamer. I
think the example I found is somewhat bloated, and is specific for
Lyx. I wrote a beamer demo based on the minimal example (the first
demo). I think for a lot of beamer users (like myself) this short
example works very well.

knitr is awesome!

best,
Paul

ps, knitr code:

\documentclass{beamer}

\begin{document}

\title{A Minimal Demo of knitr}
\author{Yihui Xie}

\maketitle

\begin{frame}[fragile]
You can test if \textbf{knitr} works with this minimal demo. OK, let's
get started with some boring random numbers:

<<boring-random>>=
set.seed(1121)
(x=rnorm(20))
mean(x);var(x)
@
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[fragile]
The first element of \texttt{x} is \Sexpr{x[1]}. Boring boxplots
and histograms recorded by the PDF device:

<<boring-plots,dev=pdf,fig.width=5,fig.height=5,out.width=.
45\linewidth,par=TRUE>>=
## two plots side by side (option fig.show=hold)
boxplot(x)
hist(x,main='')
@
\end{frame}

\end{document}

 But there must be a more elegant way to do this via hooks?

retain ...)

highlight 0.3.2 from r-forge and (2) putting show_line_numbers=TRUE into
the hack above; is there a simple/recommended way to enable this in a chunk?

    Ben Bolker

messages.subject: silly sweave
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

After years of using sweave, I'm just now starting to realize how dumb it is to create a format (Rnw) that can be read neither by neither latex nor R.

Yihui has brilliantly solved this by letting one write in vanilla latex, markdown, or html, while just sticking the code in the comments.  Would it be possible to do the reverse and write code in .R format that can be read by R, but have the markup as R-style comments using the syntax of latex, html, mardown, etc, such that an intepreter (knitr?) could read the R code and generate the desired html/pdf/etc?  (It seems this direction is closer to the original Doxygen/literate programming idea, though with Sweave-esque goal of creating dynamic documents, not just generating software documentation).  Do others think this would be useful?  Yihui, is this a possible extension of the knitr framework?

-Carl

--
Carl Boettiger
UC Davis
http://www.carlboettiger.info/

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] silly sweave
messages.body_plain:
This is somehow related to a previous feature request:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/129 In that one, we want to
write R code and all "meta information" in LaTeX comments. I said that
was my ideal model, which I have not started to pursue yet.

I think it is possible to write everything in pure R; the function
stitch() as well as read_chunk() is a simple start and still far away
from this goal.

One thing that makes this "ideal model" seem inconvenient for pure R
is how to write normal texts. For example, you probably have to use a
sequence of # to comment out a text block like this

# start_r eval=TRUE
rnorm(10) + 1
# end_r

# I want
# to say
# something
# other than R

This looks cumbersome if there is a large amount of texts to write. In
that case, I'd rather use LaTeX or HTML directly. For small-scale
scripts, stitch() may be a good start. You can also externalize R
scripts as much as possible
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/), so you can run code
freely in separate files.

BTW, it was not Sweave that invented <<>>= and @ (bottom of
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/), and it is undeniable that
Sweave has played an important role in history, so let's not say silly
:) In other places, though, this kind of home-made syntax seems to be
adopted by R, which I really dislike very much; two typical examples
are \dontrun{} and \donttest{} -- they can appear in Rd examples but
are not valid R code.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

Hi Yihui, list,

Good points, the lack of block commenting in R does make that more annoying, though with a decent text editor it shouldn't be too much of an issue.  I think it would be useful if something like your mock-up below was possible.

Didn't mean to blame sweave, but cweb/noweb's introduction of a third language and formating seemed nicely avoided by subsequent literate programming like doxygen, while it's maintained in the sweave model ;)  Does anyone actually still use noweb?

On a more practical level, is it possible to have markdown R blocks appear as markdown codeblocks (or github-flavor-markdown code-blocks?)  instead of as html comments?  It's seems it might be nice to display the code on the source copy?

Carl

On Mon, Feb 13, 2012 at 6:51 PM, Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> This is somehow related to a previous feature request:
> https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/129 In that one, we want to
> write R code and all "meta information" in LaTeX comments. I said that
> was my ideal model, which I have not started to pursue yet.
>
> I think it is possible to write everything in pure R; the function
> stitch() as well as read_chunk() is a simple start and still far away
> from this goal.
>
> One thing that makes this "ideal model" seem inconvenient for pure R
> is how to write normal texts. For example, you probably have to use a
> sequence of # to comment out a text block like this
>
> # start_r eval=TRUE
> rnorm(10) + 1
> # end_r
>
> # I want
> # to say
> # something
> # other than R
>
> This looks cumbersome if there is a large amount of texts to write. In
> that case, I'd rather use LaTeX or HTML directly. For small-scale
> scripts, stitch() may be a good start. You can also externalize R
> scripts as much as possible
> (http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/), so you can run code
> freely in separate files.
>
> BTW, it was not Sweave that invented <<>>= and @ (bottom of
> http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/), and it is undeniable that
> Sweave has played an important role in history, so let's not say silly
> :) In other places, though, this kind of home-made syntax seems to be
> adopted by R, which I really dislike very much; two typical examples
> are \dontrun{} and \donttest{} -- they can appear in Rd examples but
> are not valid R code.
>
> Regards,
> Yihui
> --
> Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
> Phone: 515-294-2465 Web: http://yihui.name
> Department of Statistics, Iowa State University
> 2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA
>
>
>
> On Mon, Feb 13, 2012 at 7:06 PM, Carl Boettiger <cboe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > After years of using sweave, I'm just now starting to realize how dumb it is
> > to create a format (Rnw) that can be read neither by neither latex nor R.
> >
> > Yihui has brilliantly solved this by letting one write in vanilla latex,
> > markdown, or html, while just sticking the code in the comments.  Would it
> > be possible to do the reverse and write code in .R format that can be read
> > by R, but have the markup as R-style comments using the syntax of latex,
> > html, mardown, etc, such that an intepreter (knitr?) could read the R code
> > and generate the desired html/pdf/etc?  (It seems this direction is closer
> > to the original Doxygen/literate programming idea, though with Sweave-esque
> > goal of creating dynamic documents, not just generating software
> > documentation).  Do others think this would be useful?  Yihui, is this a
> > possible extension of the knitr framework?
> >
> > -Carl
> >
> > --
> > Carl Boettiger
> > UC Davis
> > http://www.carlboettiger.info/
> >

--
Carl Boettiger
UC Davis
http://www.carlboettiger.info/

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] silly sweave
messages.body_plain:
I do not know if anybody still uses cweb or noweb; I knew Sweave way
before I knew these ancient inventions. I was in kindergarten when
noweb was created... It was unfortunate that Sweave was a well-behaved
student of WEB, which has created a lot of inertia so it is difficult
to abandon the original syntax.

As for markdown codeblocks, the difficulty is to be able to identify
which block is *R* code since you cannot guarantee all are R code;
that is why we need a special marker. Besides, there has to be a way
to specify chunk options. That said, I believe it is possible to
customize the regexp patterns (http://yihui.name/knitr/patterns) so
that GFM and Jekyll code blocks can be identified because both have
beginning and ending patterns (like ```r and ```). For traditional
markdown (indent 4 spaces), it is not impossible either; you may end
up with

    begin_r: label, opt1=value1, opt2=value2
    rnorm(100)
    end_r

and tell knitr your patterns are '^[ ]{4}begin_r:(.*)' and '^[ ]{4}end_r'.

If you need a concrete example, just let me know.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.body_plain:
You could use git and block tex files.  Rnw files contains documentation.  Write code in a separate R file.  R code can then be included in the document by defining a new variable

<<setup, echo = FALSE>>
REVIEW <- TRUE
@

Then use:

\SweaveOps{echo =  REVIEW}

Easy code inclusion in the text file.  This works most easily if there is just one switch, i.e. all code or no code + 'hardcoded' echo values.

Have you seen this page:
   http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/

messages.subject: Knitting standalone child documents
messages.body_plain:
The input of child files into the main document is great for organization, but sometimes it's desirable to have standalone child documents, for when you're working on a piece and it's isolated from the rest of a big main document.

I know this is why you have the eval flag to turn ON and OFF certain pieces from the main document, but is there a way to make Knitr work with the standalone or subfiles packages?

It would greatly improve workflow.

In fact, what I need could be achieved without those packages. Let me suggest a simple solution.

We could have an option for a parent in the child's \SweaveOpts, or as a comment.

-------- child-doc.Rnw --------
\SweaveOpts{parent=../main.Rnw}
% your typical child content
-------------------------------

or

-------- child-doc.Rnw --------
% knitr.parent ../main.Rnw
% your typical child content
-------------------------------

What Knitr would do is if this file is being compiled directly through knit(input), the file would be decorated with the parent's preamble (including \begin{document} and \end{document}), before compiling. However if the file is being compiled through knit_child(..., eval = TRUE), the parent option would be ignored and nothing else changed from what you have now.

I use TeXShop and made a Knitr.engine (based off of Sweave.sh <http://ggorjan.blogspot.com/2008/04/sweave-bash-shell-script.html>), that allows me to work on the document and press Cmd+T to typeset and show the resulting PDF while cleaning aux files in one go. The way you have it now I need to switch to the main.Rnw to compile and manage the toggles for eval.

The document I'm working on will get pretty big, with over 100 child documents and this gets hard to manage.

Related:
The Subfiles package <http://mirror.ctan.org/macros/latex/contrib/subfiles/subfiles.pdf>
The Standalone Package <http://mirror.ctan.org/macros/latex/contrib/standalone/standalone.pdf>

Thank you for your excellent work!

messages.subject: Re: Knitting standalone child documents
messages.body_plain:
There's a problem in running standalone child files, tucked in a subdirectory, because the relative paths of related files (produced graphics, .dat files for R.scan(), etc) won't match with the main document.

The standalone package gives an \ifstandalone conditional macro but in this case it would be great if you could solve this problem in a smarter way. A much simpler solution in our case would be through some sort of base dir prefix (which can be automatically extracted from <<child=[base_dir_for_this_child]/child.Rnw>>=), which can be accessed in our child documents (including in R code?), or through parsing and replacing some string before knitting.

This way that path could be used in case of knitting from the main file or set to ./ (or just ignored) in case of running standalone, allowing child documents to have related files all tucked in dedicated subdirectories.

My project will have a lot of files and I'm trying to keep it all organized.

Thanks!
Helder

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Knitting standalone child documents
messages.body_plain:
I think I have sorted all these issues out now. See the last section
in http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/child/. The latest version is on
GitHub.

This feature request brought much sanity to me on the file management.
In the past, my brain was a mess but now things are clearer: all input
(data, child documents) paths are relative to the Rnw file, and all
output files (tex files, figures, cache) are relative to the current
working directory. In your case, you can create a directory to store
the output, e.g.

./input/
  - main.Rnw (contains knit_child('child.Rnw') and read.csv('data.csv'))
  - child.Rnw
  - data.csv
./output/

You can setwd() to ./output/ first, then call knit('../main.Rnw'), and
you get output like this:

./output/
  - cache/
  - figure/
  - main.tex
  - child.tex

For child.Rnw, you can call set_parent('main.Rnw') so it borrows
preamble from main.Rnw; not set_parent() is aware of whether the
current child document is compiled as a child document or a standalone
document, so you can use it freely.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

Cool, I can run standalone files now :)

I actually had the following structure in mind for my project:

main.Rnw
main.pdf
  - chap1/
    - ex1/
      - ex1.Rnw
      - ex1.dat
      - ex1.pdf
    - ex2/
      - ex2.Rnw
      - ex2.pdf
  - chap2/
    ...

But what you suggest is simpler and also solves another problem for me which is cleaning up after the deed. Nice :)

I got it to work automatically in TeXShop for the main.Rnw, but I have a problem in standalone files.

I have this now:

main.Rnw
child1.Rnw
child2.Rnw
output/

With this parent in child1.Rnw...

<<setup-child1>>=
set_parent("main.Rnw")
@

Running...

> library(knitr); setwd('output'); knit('../child1.Rnw')

Which outputs...

main.Rnw
child1.Rnw
child2.Rnw
output/
  - child1.tex
  - figure/

Running child1.tex gives the following error...

! LaTeX Error: \usepackage before \documentclass.

In fact when I inspect child1.tex, the preamble from main.Rnw isn't being copied.

As an aside, is it possible to have the child doc run chunks from the main doc, as well as inherit global chunk options from \SweaveOpts? The reason is that I now have a few duplicates for setting knit_hooks$set(crop=hook_pdfcrop) and library(xtable), for example, in every child. It would be great to have this duplication removed.

Thanks!
Helder

messages.subject: Summary of my knitr customizations
messages.body_plain:
With an amazing amount of assistance from Yihui I have been very
successful in customizing knitr to make good use of the listings
package and to automatically create figure environments when a
caption= parameter is specified inside <<>>=.  I have slightly updated
the Sweavel LaTeX style file at http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/wiki/pub/Main/SweaveTemplate/Sweavel.sty,
and I use the following knitr hooks/customizations:

# All this goes into file setup.r
spar <- function(mar=if(!axes)
                 c(2.25+bot-.45*multi,1.5+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.5+rt)
else
                 c(3.25+bot-.45*multi,3.5+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.
5+rt),
                 lwd = if(multi)1 else 1.75,
                 mgp = if(!axes) mgp=c(.75, .1, 0) else
                       if(multi) c(1.5, .365, 0) else c(2.4-.4, 0.475,
0),
                 tcl = if(multi)-0.25 else -0.4,
                 bot=0, left=0, top=0, rt=0, ps=if(multi) 14 else 10,
                 mfrow=NULL, axes=TRUE, ...)
  {
    multi <- length(mfrow) > 0
    par(mar=mar, lwd=lwd, mgp=mgp, tcl=tcl, ps=ps, ...)
    if(multi) par(mfrow=mfrow)
  }

knit_hooks$set(chunk = function(x, options) x) # do not wrap output in
kframe
## for those who read source code here: I cannot use echo=TRUE here
because
## the code \begin{lstlistings} and \end{lstlistings} will confuse the
## listings package and cause LaTeX errors

hook_lst_bf = function(x, options)
  paste('\\begin{lstlisting}[basicstyle={\\bfseries}]\n', x,
        '\\end{lstlisting}\n', sep = '')
## Scode and Soutput are defined in Sweavel.sty using listings

unlink('messages.txt') # Start fresh with each run
hook_log = function(x, options) cat(x, file='messages.txt',
append=TRUE)

knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options)
               paste('\\begin{Scode}\n', x, '\\end{Scode}\n', sep=''),
               output = function(x, options)
               paste('\\begin{Soutput}\n', x, '\\end{Soutput}\n',
sep=''),
               warning = hook_log, message = hook_log, error =
hook_lst_bf)
set_header(highlight = '')

knit_hooks$set(plot=function (x, options) {
  if (!options$include)
    return("")
  ## Begin FH
  cap <- options$caption
  bfig <- efig <- ''
  if(length(cap)) {
    if(is.na <http://is.na>(cap)) cap <- ''
    lp <- options$label.prefix
    lab <- paste(lp, options$label, sep='')
    bfig <- sprintf('\\begin{figure}\\label{%s}\n', lab)
    scap <- options$scaption
    scap <- if(!length(scap) || is.na <http://is.na>(scap)) '' else
     paste('[', scap, ']', sep='')
    efig <- sprintf('\\caption%s{\\smaller %s}\n\\end{figure}\n',
scap, cap)
  } # End FH
  rw = options$resize.width
  rh = options$resize.height
  resize1 = resize2 = ""
  if (!is.null(rw) || !is.null(rh)) {
    resize1 = sprintf("\\resizebox{%s}{%s}{", ifelse(is.null(rw),
      "!", rw), ifelse(is.null(rh), "!", rh))
    resize2 = "} "
  }
  tikz <- FALSE # FH
  a = options$fig.align
  fig.cur = options$fig.cur
  fig.num = options$fig.num
  if (is.null(fig.cur))
    fig.cur = 0L
  animate = options$fig.show == "animate"
  if (!tikz && animate && fig.cur < fig.num)
    return("")
  align1 = switch(a, left = "\n\n", center = "\n\n\\centering{}",
    right = "\n\n\\hfill{}", "")
  align2 = switch(a, left = "\\hfill{}\n\n", center = "\n\n",
    right = "\n\n", "")
  hold = options$fig.show == "hold"
  if (hold && fig.cur > 1L)
    align1 = ""
  if (hold && fig.cur > 0L && fig.cur < fig.num)
    align2 = ""
  size = paste(c(sprintf("width=%s", options$out.width),
sprintf("height=%s",
    options$out.height)), collapse = ",")
  paste(bfig, align1, resize1, if (tikz) {   # FH added bfig,
    sprintf("\\input{%s.tikz}", x[1])
  }
  else if (animate) {
    aniopts = options$aniopts
    aniopts = if (is.na <http://is.na>(aniopts))
      NULL
    else gsub(";", ",", aniopts)
    if (nzchar(size))
      size = paste(size, sprintf("%s", aniopts), sep = ",")
    if (nzchar(size))
      size = sprintf("[%s]", size)
    sprintf("\\animategraphics%s{%s}{%s}{%s}{%s}", size,
            1/options$interval, sub(str_c(fig.num, "$"), "",
                                    x[1]), 1L, fig.num)
  }
  else {
    if (nzchar(size))
      size = sprintf("[%s]", size)
    sprintf("\\includegraphics%s{%s} ", size, x[1])
  }, resize2, align2, efig, sep = "")  # FH added efig,
})

knit_hooks$set(par=function(before, options, envir)
               if(before && options$fig.show != 'none')
               {
                 p <-
c('bty','mfrow','ps','bot','top','left','rt','lwd',
                        'mgp','tcl', 'axes')
                 pars <- opts_current$get(p)
                 pars <- pars[!is.na <http://is.na>(names(pars))]
                 if(length(pars)) do.call('spar', pars) else spar()
               })

opts_knit$set(eval.opts = c('eval', 'echo', 'caption', 'scaption',
                'mfrow', 'mgp', 'tcl'))
## allows symbolic captions, mfrow, etc., short captions for table of
figures
## see http://yihui.name/knitr/options#package_options
## Allow symbolic mfrom, mgp, etc. because user may specify e.g.
c(1,2)
options(replace.assign=TRUE)

I don't put warnings in the report output but rather to a separate
file messages.txt

In knit_hooks$set(plot=function ....) see lines marked with FH to see
what I changed over what is provided with knitr.

Then in my individual documents I use:

<<echo=FALSE>>=
source('../setup.r')
@

\SweaveOpts{highlight=FALSE, fig.path=PREFIX-, fig.align=center,
fig.width=4, fig.height=3, fig.show=hold, comment=NA,
label.prefix=fig:gen-, par=TRUE}

. . .
<<rcscomp,mfrow=c(1\,2),fig.height=4,fig.width=6,caption="Restricted
cubic spline component variables for $k = 5$ and knots at $X = .05\, .
275\, .5\, .725$\, and $.95$. The left panel is a $y$--magnification
of the right panel.  Fitted functions such as those in Figure \
\ref{fig:gen-rcsex} will be linear combinations of these basis
functions as long as knots are at the same locations used
here.",scaption="Restricted cubic spline component variables for 5
knots">>=
. . .
@

<<rcsex,fig.height=6,fig.width=7,bot=2,mfrow=c(2\,
2),ps=13,caption="Some typical restricted cubic spline functions for
$k = 3\, 4\, 5\, 6$.  The $y$--axis is $X\\beta$.  Arrows indicate
knots. These curves were derived by randomly choosing values of $\\beta
$ subject to standard deviations of fitted functions being
normalized.",scaption="Some typical restricted cubic spline
functions">>=
. . .
@

You can also stuff captions into R variables in earlier chunks then
call out the caption with caption=variable name in a later chunk.

I'm very pleased with how this is working and plan to re-do my book
using this approach.

Thanks to Yihui and others who have helped so much.  If any of this
becomes built-in to knitr I'll have even less work to do next time.

Frank

messages.subject: chunk headers, more like R's lazy formals?
messages.subject_clean: chunk headers, more like R's lazy formals?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Escaping commas in pseudo-R expressions such as keep=c(1\, 3\, 5)
feels a bit awkward and inconsistent (contrast with
background=.97;.97;1), so I was curious to know why commas (and
spaces) are so problematic in knitr's chunk options. I suspect it's
got something to do with the way those options are parsed,

https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/R/parser.R#L76

    pieces = str_split(str_replace_all(pieces, fixed('\\,'), ','), '=', n = 2L)

Now, I wonder if it wouldn't be more flexible to match a list of known
chunk options (the full list is presumably available at via
opts_chunk$get()), rather than using a fixed format strsplit. In fact,
to my (probably naive) eyes, the chunk header looks a lot like the
formals() of an R function

formals(ls)
$name

$pos
-1

$envir
as.environment(pos)

$all.names
[1] FALSE

$pattern

Perhaps this analogy could be pursued further by enforcing that all
chunk parameters be valid R expressions, and ultimately used to work
around the current limitations?

Just a thought anyway!

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.subject_clean: [knitr] chunk headers, more like R's lazy formals?
messages.body_plain:
Well, after experimenting with this idea for a while, I should say
this is very doable and will be a fantastic solution. All chunk
options can go to valid R code (character values should be quoted, and
R expressions like c(1, 3, 4) can be used freely). I feel lucky I did
not release the current version to CRAN today, otherwise I will surely
regret it.

However, this will introduce a nasty backward compatibility issue,
because I went astray from the very beginning, treating with chunk
options as a character string instead of function arguments.
Internally I will have to fix options like background=.97;.97;.97 to
background=c(.97,.97,.97), and fig.path=foo/bar- to
fig.path="foo/bar-".

I'm quite happy about this finding, and I believe Frank will find this
solution satisfactory as well, although the experimental feature \,
has to be dropped which will bring a little bit more manual work to
him to replace \, back to ,.

Regards,

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Knitting standalone child documents
messages.body_plain:
\SweaveOpts{} in the preamble of the parent document is also parsed
when knitting a child document in the standalone mode. And
\SweaveOpts{} just acts like you described: it takes effect from the
point where it is called, so the order matters; set_parent() parses it
in the parent preamble, so the \SweaveOpts{} in the parent preamble is
used when set_parent() is called. It is similar to the function
options(): whenever it is called, the options are changed globally and
permanently in this R session.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: knitr and Eclipse
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am having a fantastic time watching knitr develop - it seems that
every day, someone has asked for - and received! - a new feature that
I can use. I am working in the Eclipse environment, and am finding
knitr far more Eclipse-friendly than was pgfSweave. In particular, the
ability to knit tex documents means that I can make use of Eclipse's
excellent outlining and word-wrapping features for the tex document
(the lack of outlining for rnw was particularly annoying) and the R
documents also have a nice outline feature in addition to the object
list and other good things.

I see mention of support for RStudio, so I thought I should say that
Eclipse already plays quite nicely with knitr.

Thanks again for all your good work, Yihui.

I have been messing with knitr some more trying to get the output that I need.  My last blog post on r.andrewredd.us <http://r.andrewredd.us>, the one on dostats package, was built with knitr using markdown.  I ran into a few problems with it.  First my site is configured to use GeSHI for highlighting R code wrapped in a <pre lang="r"> tag.  but I don't get that from knitr.  I do get some marked up code, but without the stylesheet is fairly useless.

I was able to make a work around with using `render_gfm()` to get the "```r" syntax that I fed into pandoc that produced similar highlighted code but also included the stylesheet that I was able to configure on my server.  Neither of these are things that I particularly like.  I was trying to do several things that I have not been able to figure out. It would be great if we can figure out how to do these and put them up on the wiki on github for others.  I feel like the hooks, patterns, etc. are not documented enough to do this.

Change the output format to do other things like <pre lang="r"> or output like pandoc format with carrying over attributes.(http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/demo/example9/pandocs-markdown.html)
Change the patterns to include other things such as  "```r" for markdown with eval=FALSE as the default so that "```r eval=T" is required for evaluating code.  To be more accurate to markdown the pattern should be something like "^`{3,}\s*r"
Change the file extension defaults such as .rmd for r laced markdown.  I personally dislike the _knit_ pattern since with the tools I use on a daily basis that is hard to strip off where the extension is very easy to strip off.
It would be great if there were some examples in the wiki of how to do this, or at least somewhere.  Also the wiki would be a great place to collect these patterns for other document types so that people can build up a library.

-Andrew

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Summary of my knitr customizations
messages.body_plain:
I have implemented the new syntax for options now.

'eval.opts' has been deprecated because it does not make any sense to
the new syntax: all options will be evaluated if they are not
constants (numeric, character, logical, ...), but some options can be
postponed by the package option 'eval.after'. In your case, you can
set

opts_knit$set(eval.after = 'fig.cap')

The new syntax requires all options to be valid R code, so strings
must be quoted, and backslashes in strings must be escaped as \\ (e.g.
"\\textwidth").

To other knitr users: I'm in the process of updating all
documentations, and when I'm done, I will point you all to a page of
the comparison between new and old syntax of writing chunk options.
Good news is that I have kept maximum backward compatibility: if new
syntax fails, old syntax will be used, so there should not be horrible
transition problems.

Regards,
Yihui

Working great now.

knitr has come at a great time for me as I'm updating a 300-page short
course handout and re-writing my book.  I'm converting both to knitr.
The elegance of how knitr implements the listings package, the LaTeX
figure environment, labels, and captions is stunning.  Thanks for all
your great efforts Yihui!

Soon I'll modify our Sweave publication-ready template at
http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/SweaveTemplate to list my knitr
setup.  The current setup is below:

spar <- function(mar=if(!axes)
                 c(2.25+bot-.45*multi,2+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.5+rt)

else
                 c(3.25+bot-.45*multi,3.5+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.
5+rt),
                 lwd = if(multi)1 else 1.75,
                 mgp = if(!axes) mgp=c(.75, .1, 0) else
                       if(multi) c(1.5, .365, 0) else c(2.4-.4, 0.475,
0),
                 tcl = if(multi)-0.25 else -0.4,
                 bot=0, left=0, top=0, rt=0, ps=if(multi) 14 else 10,
                 mfrow=NULL, axes=TRUE, ...)
  {
    multi <- length(mfrow) > 0
    par(mar=mar, lwd=lwd, mgp=mgp, tcl=tcl, ps=ps, ...)
    if(multi) par(mfrow=mfrow)
  }

render_listings()

unlink('messages.txt') # Start fresh with each run
hook_log = function(x, options) cat(x, file='messages.txt',
append=TRUE)

knit_hooks$set(warning = hook_log, message = hook_log)

knit_hooks$set(par=function(before, options, envir)
               if(before && options$fig.show != 'none')
               {
                 p <-
c('bty','mfrow','ps','bot','top','left','rt','lwd',
                        'mgp','tcl', 'axes')
                 pars <- opts_current$get(p)
                 pars <- pars[!is.na <http://is.na>(names(pars))]
                 if(length(pars)) do.call('spar', pars) else spar()
               })

opts_knit$set(aliases=c(h='fig.height', w='fig.width',
                cap='fig.cap', scap='fig.scap'))

opts_knit$set(eval.after = c('fig.cap','fig.scap'))

\SweaveOpts{fig.path='chaptername-', fig.align='center', w=4, h=3,
fig.show='hold', fig.lp='fig:chaptername-', par=TRUE, tidy=FALSE}

messages.subject: knitr 0.3 is ready
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I planned to release knitr 0.3 one week ago, but baptiste mentioned a
useful new feature (https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/142) which I
really wanted to bring to the new version, so I went ahead and
implemented it. Briefly speaking, this feature means your chunk
options will be parsed as R code instead of a text string, e.g.

<<mychunk, eval=dothis, echo=c(1, 3), fig.cap=paste('the value of pi is', pi)>>=

this gives you full power of options; you can pass anything to chunk
options, and this will greatly extend the power of hooks as well.

I also tried to keep backward compatibility: if your chunk options are
not valid R code, the old way of parsing will still be used. I tested
it on all my manuals, it worked fine with old options, so I guess it
will not bring much trouble to you. More details at:
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/sweave/

Other news at: https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS

Before I release the new version to CRAN, I'd like to ask you to test
it to see if there are fatal compatibility issues. I do not want to
see furious knitters jumping over me if this new version breaks their
old documents. Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Phone: 515-294-2465 Web: http://yihui.name
Department of Statistics, Iowa State University
2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: knitr 0.3 is ready
messages.body_plain:
Well, what you described is exactly what I have been thinking when I
was developing knitr. In the beginning, I only work with single
documents (no children or parents), so I set the output directory to
be the same as these documents by default. Later, I received more and
more requests about child documents, and I began to feel this was not
a good default. It is much cleaner not to tie input with output.

In the past I did not like setwd() to long directory names either, but
later my practice changed: I always start R (in the terminal) in the
directory in which I want to work, so I do not need to wrestle with
setwd() frequently. In your case, I would do this:

cd ~/Desktop/temp/
R
library(knitr)
knit('file.Rnw')

But you are probably using R.app under Mac, so you have to change the
working directory after you start the GUI. I tend to recommend useRs
to learn this by heart:

Man, know thy getwd()!

-----

If you still find this messy, I have another weapon for you (read the
second paragraph of my reply):
https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=en&fromgroups#!topic/knitr/f9WuyKszW7c

You can call knitr via command line after you added the executable
'knit' to your PATH:

cd ~/Desktop/temp/
knit file.Rnw --pdf

In this case, you do not need to open R at all.

-----

If this still sounds horrible, I bet RStudio should be handy:
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/rstudio/ This boils down to one single
click from Rnw to PDF.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Parsing bug
messages.body_plain:
should be results='tex', or better, results='asis'

knitr will issue errors or warnings whenever the new syntax fails, but
usually it does not matter, because it will just roll back to the old
way of paring options

To know the class of an option, see http://yihui.name/knitr/options
(e.g. results should be character)

However, in your case, the failure was a real failure, because when
knitr rolled back to the old syntax, it found commas in your words,
which should be escaped. Therefore neither the new nor the old syntax
could work for you.

Another problem is, you want to write \{ in TeX, which means you need
to write \\{ in R, which in turn means \\\\{ in the chunk option. This
is similar to how we write \ in regular expressions in R; please let
me know if you need more explanations.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.body_plain:
In chunks such as

<<iacholxage-2,results=tex,h=5,w=7,cap=Restricted cubic spline fit
with age $\\times$ spline(cholesterol) and cholesterol $\\times$
spline(age)>>=

where the value of cap is not a legal R expression but has no commas,
the latest knitr parses cap correctly.  If I enclose the caption in
quotes such as cap='Restricted ...(age)', knitr will include the
quotes in the LaTeX output, e.g. \caption{'Restricted cubic ...'}.  It
would be helpful if knitr could ignore single or double quotes that
start or end an expression.

If the expression contains one or more commas, knitr requires the
expression to be in quotes, and the quotes are handled correctly by
suppressing them from \caption.

Frank

messages.body_plain:
Again, the real reason is results should be 'tex', since tex is not an
R variable. Just imagine you are writing function arguments; what is
this supposed to mean?

my_function_call(h = 5, results = tex, cap = 'hello, caption')

In the new syntax, you no longer worry about commas. You do whatever
you can do in R function arguments.

It may take a while to remember which options should be characters,
though, because we have been writing results=tex for many years. The
rule of thumb is, whenever the option is not numeric or logical, it
probably should be quoted.

Regards,

messages.subject: par called twice per plot?
messages.body_plain:
In my setup:

spar <- function(mar=if(!axes)
                 c(2.25+bot-.45*multi,2+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.5+rt)
else
                 c(3.25+bot-.45*multi,3.5+left,.5+top+.25*multi,.
5+rt),
                 lwd = if(multi)1 else 1.75,
                 mgp = if(!axes) mgp=c(.75, .1, 0) else
                       if(multi) c(1.5, .365, 0) else c(2.4-.4, 0.475,
0),
                 tcl = if(multi)-0.25 else -0.4,
                 bot=0, left=0, top=0, rt=0, ps=if(multi) 14 else 10,
                 mfrow=NULL, axes=TRUE, ...)
  {
    multi <- length(mfrow) > 0
    par(mar=mar, lwd=lwd, mgp=mgp, tcl=tcl, ps=ps, ...)
    if(multi) par(mfrow=mfrow)
  }

knit_hooks$set(par=function(before, options, envir)
               if(before && options$fig.show != 'none')
               {
                 p <-
c('bty','mfrow','ps','bot','top','left','rt','lwd',
                        'mgp','tcl', 'axes')
                 pars <- opts_current$get(p)
                 pars <- pars[!is.na <http://is.na>(names(pars))]
                 if(length(pars)) do.call('spar', pars) else spar()
               })

\SweaveOpts{fig.path='titanic-', fig.align='center', w=4.5, h=3.5,
fig.show='hold', fig.lp='fig:titanic-', par=TRUE, tidy=FALSE}

I do thinks like <<myplot,rt=4>>=
rt=4 adds 4 to the default right margin in mar() (done by spar).

But I think I'm seeing spar() called twice per chunk, with the second
call ignoring rt=4.  This second call seems to be the one that
matters, so rt is effectively ignored.

Does that make sense?  Is there a workaround?  Should I be
conditioning on "before" in knit_hooks$set(par=...) ?

Thanks
Frank

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] par called twice per plot?
messages.body_plain:
You have already conditioned on 'if (before && ...)'. I checked your
par hook, and I saw it was only called once per chunk. It is easy to
verify that by returning a character string in your chunk hook, e.g.

knit_hooks$set(par = function... {
  if (...) {
    ...
    return('I was called once...') # this string will be written into tex output
  }
})

If it was called twice, you will see two strings in the beginning and
end of a chunk respectively.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Re: par called twice per plot?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Yihui.  Returning a character string is a useful debugging
tool.  I see the problem now.  spar() was being called for every code
chunk even if no plot was produced.  I assume that doesn't cause any
problem with graphics rendering for chunks that do produce plots.  But
spar() was only called once per chunk, as you said.

I am having a weird problem with the right margin of a graphic being
different with knitr than with a manually run pdf(...)
Here's a small test program if you have time to take a look.  The
auxdata argument to dotchart2 in the Hmisc package causes some extra
right margin to be added with par, then right-justifies auxdata in the
right margin.  test.pdf is not equal to test2.pdf.

\SweaveOpts{fig.width=4.5, fig.height=3.5}
<<test>>=
require(Hmisc)
# 100 200 300 runs into the figure box right side
dotchart2(1:3, labels=c('a','b','c'), auxdata=(1:3)*100)
@

<<>>=
# Works - 100 200 300 properly set in right margin
pdf('test2.pdf', width=4.5, height=3.5)
require(Hmisc)
dotchart2(1:3, labels=c('a','b','c'), auxdata=(1:3)*100)
dev.off()
@

Thanks again,
Frank

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: par called twice per plot?
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Re: par called twice per plot?
messages.body_plain:
This is somehow expected. To illustrate the problem, you can draw the
plot in an x11() window and resize the window to different sizes. You
will notice the three labels 100, 200 and 300 do not keep a constant
relative distance to the plot frame box: when the plot window is
narrow, they can go inside the plot region. In other words, auxdata
was drawn with a metric that does not scale well.

Now, the problem is knitr records the plot with a null device, of
which the dimension is not clear to me, but I suppose it should be
different with 4.5x3.5 inches. When you save the plot object with the
pdf() device, the labels on the right can be moved to a different
relative location. I'm not sure if Hmisc::outerText can be adjusted to
deal with this situation (e.g. does axis(side = 4) help?).

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Re: par called twice per plot?
messages.body_plain:
That was a huge help Yihui.  The dotchart2 and outerText functions
have been problematic for me for years, and I never stopped to think
about text( ) not preserving the right relative location upon
stretching the device window.  I re-wrote outerText to use mtext()
instead, and now the right margin text location is preserved under
stretching.

Thanks yet again!
Frank
